title: A Dichotomy for MIP* in the Presence of Unital Noise
authors: Yangjing Dong, Zhenyu Jiang, Minglong Qin, Penghui Yao, Haigang Zhou
abstract: A recent work studied quantum two-prover one-round proof systems $\mathsf{MIP}^ψ[\text{poly},O(1)]$. It showed that when $ψ$ is a noisy EPR state with quantum maximal correlation $ρ_{\max}(ψ)<1$, the resulting complexity class is equivalent to $\mathsf{NEXP}=\mathsf{MIP}$. In contrast, $\mathsf{MIP}^{\text{EPR}}[\text{poly},O(1)]=\mathsf{RE}$. Not all noise, however, decreases quantum maximal correlation. A basic example is dephasing noise: a dephased EPR pair retain quantum maximal correlation $1$. In this work, we remove the constant-answer restriction and establish a complete dichotomy for $\mathsf{MIP}^ψ[\text{poly},\text{poly}]$, where the provers share arbitrarily many copies of EPR pairs subject to unital noise. Equivalently, let $ψ$ be a fixed two-qubit state with maximally mixed marginals. We prove that \[\mathsf{MIP}^ψ[\text{poly},\text{poly}]=\mathsf{MIP} =\mathsf{NEXP},~\text{if $ψ$ is separable or $ρ_{\max}(ψ)<1$};\]\[\mathsf{MIP}^ψ[\text{poly},\text{poly}]=\mathsf{MIP}^ψ[\text{poly},O(1)]=\mathsf{RE},\text{if $ψ$ is entangled and $ρ_{\max}(ψ)=1$.}\] Beyond the complexity classification, our proof develops two techniques that may be useful more broadly in quantum information and quantum complexity. First, we introduce a positivity-preserving low-degree approximation framework for quantum measurements: instead of truncating positive operators directly in the Pauli basis, we approximate suitable square-root factorizations, simultaneously achieving low Pauli degree, positivity, and global control over an entire POVM. Second, we develop a new dimension-reduction method, called Pauli folding, for low-degree positive operators. Its key ingredient is an almost-multiplicativity theorem for randomized Pauli hashing, which allows noncommutative products, positivity, and normalization to survive compression with controlled error.
summary: This work determines the exact computational power of quantum interactive proofs ($	ext{MIP}_{\psi}$) when the shared resource is a noisy two-qubit state $\psi$. It proves a sharp dichotomy: the system is classically bounded ($	ext{NEXP}$) unless the state is highly entangled with perfect correlation ($ho_{\max}(\psi)=1$), in which case it achieves the full power of $	ext{RE}$. The paper also introduces advanced mathematical tools for analyzing quantum measurements.
main_problem: The paper establishes a complete dichotomy for the computational power of the quantum two-prover one-round proof system $	ext{MIP}_{\psi}[	ext{poly}, 	ext{poly}]$ based on the properties of the shared noisy quantum state $\psi$.
main_result: The computational power collapses to $	ext{NEXP}=	ext{MIP}$ if the state $\psi$ is separable or has low quantum maximal correlation ($ho_{\max}(\psi)<1$); however, if $\psi$ is entangled and $ho_{\max}(\psi)=1$, the power reaches $	ext{RE}$.
method: The proof develops novel techniques including a positivity-preserving low-degree approximation framework for quantum measurements and a dimension-reduction method called Pauli folding.
model_or_system: The model is the two-prover one-round interactive proof system ($	ext{MIP}_{\psi}$), where the provers share arbitrarily many copies of a fixed two-qubit state $\psi$ subject to unital noise.
key_observables: Quantum maximal correlation $ho_{\max}(\psi)$, separability of $\psi$, and the resulting complexity class ($	ext{NEXP}$ vs $	ext{RE}$).
important_parameters: The structure of the shared state $\psi$ (two-qubit, maximally mixed marginals), and the bounds on question/answer lengths ($	ext{poly}$ vs $O(1)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the shared state $\psi$ has maximally mixed marginals and focuses on the dichotomy based on $ho_{\max}(\psi)$ and entanglement.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews previous results for constant-answer regimes, then establishes the complete dichotomy for polynomial answer lengths, and finally details the two main technical contributions: the low-degree approximation framework and Pauli folding.
why_interesting: The development of the positivity-preserving low-degree approximation framework and Pauli folding offers general tools for analyzing quantum measurements and non-commutative structures, which are highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum error correction.
